NEW YORK (CNN) — The bond between Kanye West and his mother, Donda, is evident simply by listening to his songs. Donda and Kanye West, shown together during her book tour, shared a very close relationship.

Kanye often mentioned his mother in his lyrics, touching on subjects ranging from her desire for him to earn a college degree to her unwavering encouragement when he eventually chose to build a career in rap.

Donda West, who died over the weekend at age 58, came across as both strong-willed and deeply affectionate. In “Can’t Tell Me Nothing,” a song from his newest album, *Graduation*, Kanye raps about his mother trying to stop him from spending money on jewelry and “Louis V.” In “Touch the Sky,” from his 2005 album *Late Registration*, he remembers her driving him from Chicago, Illinois, to New York in a U-Haul truck.

She also inspired “Hey Mama,” another song from *Late Registration*. In it, Kanye raps, “I want to scream so loud for you / because I’m so proud of you,” and continues, “I know I act a fool / but I promise you I’m going back to school / I appreciate what you allowed for me and I just want you to be proud of me.”

On “Hey Mama,” first widely known from his early mixtape era and later featured on *Late Registration*, Kanye celebrated her sacrifices and devotion, rapping with open affection about the woman who raised him and believed in him long before fame arrived. The song became one of his most beloved tributes, a rare moment of pure gratitude in a catalog often marked by ego, grief, and contradiction.

Kanye’s lyrics about his mother frequently framed her as both protector and witness: the person who saw his potential before the world did. In “Hey Mama,” he recalls childhood struggles, her hard work, and his desire to repay her with success. After her death in 2007, those lyrics took on a deeper poignancy, becoming not just a celebration but a memorial. Later songs and performances would continue to reflect the enormity of her absence, with Kanye often returning to themes of loss, family, and the emotional cost of fame.

Donda was also publicly proud of her son’s rise. She often spoke warmly about Kanye’s talent and determination, and she supported his career at a time when his path—from producer to rapper—was not guaranteed. Her pride was evident as Kanye transformed from a Chicago producer into a Grammy-winning star, first with *The College Dropout* and then with *Late Registration*. She appeared not as a distant celebrity parent, but as an active and loving force in his life.

One of the biggest moments she lived to see was the buildup to Kanye’s third album, *Graduation*, released in September 2007. The album became part of a highly publicized sales showdown with 50 Cent’s *Curtis*, as both records arrived on the same day. The rivalry was framed as a clash between two eras and styles of hip-hop: 50 Cent’s dominant gangsta-rap commercial machine versus Kanye’s more melodic, introspective, and pop-expansive vision.

The result was a turning point. *Graduation* outsold *Curtis* in its first week, a victory widely interpreted as a shift in mainstream rap’s center of gravity. Kanye’s triumph confirmed his place at the forefront of hip-hop and helped open the door for a broader emotional and musical palette in the genre. For Donda West, it was another moment of vindication—proof that the son she had encouraged and championed had not only succeeded, but helped redirect the culture.

Donda West died on November 10, 2007, at age 58, shortly after undergoing cosmetic surgery. Her sudden death devastated Kanye and became one of the most consequential personal losses of his life. In the years since, her name has remained central to his art and public identity, from songs and interviews to the title of his 2021 album *Donda*.

Her legacy endures in the music she inspired, in the pride she took in her son’s ascent, and in the emotional honesty Kanye West has often shown when speaking—or rapping—about her. For all the spectacle surrounding his career, Donda West remains one of its most human and enduring figures: the mother behind the artist, and the muse whose influence never left him.
